issues.legal_issue: A signature on an instrument counts as attestation only when the signer signs with the intention of witnessing the executant’s signature or acknowledgment and does so in the executant’s presence.
material_facts: The security bond was signed by one witness who attested it.
The registering officer signed the document while carrying out registration duties, and the evidence did not show that he signed in the executant’s presence or with an intention to attest.
The identifying witnesses signed to authenticate the executant’s identity, and the evidence did not show that they intended to attest the document.
issues.conclusion: The registering officer and identifying witnesses were not attesting witnesses, so the bond was attested by only one witness.
issues.legal_principle: Under section 3 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, attestation requires two or more witnesses who saw the executant sign or received the executant’s personal acknowledgment, and each must sign in the executant’s presence with the intention of attesting. A signature made for another purpose, such as identifying the executant or performing a registering officer’s statutory duties, does not constitute attestation. The Court relied on Girja Datt v. Gangotri, Abinash Chandra Bidyanidhi Bhattacharya v. Dasarath Malo, Shiam Sundar Singh v. Jagannath Singh, and Surendra Bahadur Singh v. Thakur Behari Singh; it held that Veerappa Chettiar v. Subramania did not establish otherwise beyond the stated requirements.

predicates.attestation_dispute: The parties disputed whether a person who signed an instrument was an attesting witness.
predicates.signer_signed_for_another_purpose: A person signed the instrument to identify the executant or perform another function rather than to witness execution.
predicates.signer_signed_with_attesting_intent: A person signed the instrument intending to witness the executant’s signature or personal acknowledgment.

issues.definition: When an attestation dispute arises, a signature made for another purpose or without attesting intent does not count as attestation.

issues.legal_issue: A charge on immovable property does not require witness attestation merely because provisions governing simple mortgages apply to the charge.
material_facts: A security bond charged immovable properties to secure payment of money.
The bond was signed by only one attesting witness but was duly registered.
The charge was created by an instrument, and the respondents argued that the bond was invalid without two attesting witnesses.
issues.conclusion: The charge did not require witness attestation; because the bond was duly registered, it was valid and operative.
issues.legal_principle: Section 100 of the Transfer of Property Act, 1882, does not import section 59’s requirements for creating a mortgage into the creation of a charge. The provision applying rules governing simple mortgages to charges concerns the rights and liabilities of the parties, not the mode of creating a charge. A non-testamentary instrument creating a charge of the relevant value must be registered under section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act, 1908, but no law requires it to be attested by witnesses. The Court approved Baburao v. Narayan and disapproved Viswanadhan v. Menon and Shiva Rao v. Shanmugasundaraswami.

rule.if: charge_validity_dispute and charge_created_by_instrument and instrument_requires_registration and instrument_registered

predicates.charge_validity_dispute: The parties disputed the validity of a charge over immovable property.
predicates.charge_created_by_instrument: A person created a charge over immovable property by executing an instrument.
predicates.instrument_requires_registration: The instrument creating the charge was of a kind that the law requires to be registered.
predicates.instrument_registered: The instrument creating the charge was registered.

issues.definition: In a dispute about an instrument-created charge, if the instrument required registration and was registered, the charge is valid without witness attestation.

issues.legal_issue: A decree that declares a security bond to be a charge and permits sale of the charged property is not reduced to a mere recital because the plaint was not amended to request enforcement of the charge.
material_facts: The security bond provided that the charged properties would secure payment of any decree in the suit.
The decree stated that the bond would enure to the decree-holder as a charge for the decretal amount and permitted an application for sale of the properties if payment was not made.
The plaintiff had not amended the plaint to add a prayer for enforcement of the charge.
The properties were subsequently sold pursuant to the decree.
issues.conclusion: The decree declared and provided for enforcement of the charge; the failure to amend the plaint was an irregularity that did not change the decree’s construction.
issues.legal_principle: The decree must be construed according to its terms and effect. An omission to amend the plaint is an irregularity that does not turn operative provisions declaring a charge and allowing sale into a mere recital.

predicates.decree_construction_dispute: The parties disputed whether a decree declared or enforced a charge created by a security instrument.
predicates.decree_identifies_bond_as_charge: The decree states that a security instrument operates as a charge for the amount due.
predicates.decree_permits_sale_to_discharge_charge: The decree permits the charged property to be sold to discharge the secured amount.

issues.definition: When a decree identifies a security instrument as a charge and permits sale to discharge it, the decree declares and provides for enforcement of that charge.

issues.legal_issue: A creditor seeking rateable distribution of proceeds from a sale on the assumption that the sale was lawful cannot challenge the court’s territorial jurisdiction to order that sale in the same proceedings.
material_facts: The properties sold under the decree were outside the territorial limits of the court’s ordinary original jurisdiction.
The respondents sought rateable distribution of the proceeds on the assumption that the properties had been lawfully sold.
The respondents’ claim to divide the proceeds depended on the sale having been lawful.
issues.conclusion: The respondents could not raise the territorial-jurisdiction objection in those proceedings; the Court did not decide whether the objection had been waived or was otherwise unavailable to the judgment-debtor.
issues.legal_principle: A party seeking division of sale proceeds on the premise that the property was lawfully sold cannot at the same time challenge the court’s jurisdiction to order that sale. In discussing the unresolved question of waiver, the Court referred to Seth Hiralal Patni v. Sri Kali Nath, Bahrein Petroleum Co. Ltd. v. P. J. Pappu, and Zamindar of Etiyapuram v. Chidambaram Chetty.

predicates.rateable_distribution_proceeding: Creditors applied to share assets realized through execution of a decree.
predicates.applicants_assume_sale_was_lawful: The applicants’ request to share the proceeds depended on treating the property sale as lawful.
predicates.applicants_challenge_sale_jurisdiction: The applicants argued that the court lacked territorial jurisdiction to order the sale.

issues.definition: In a proceeding to share execution-sale proceeds, applicants who rely on the sale as lawful cannot challenge the court’s jurisdiction to order it.

issues.legal_issue: When property is sold under a decree ordering sale to discharge an encumbrance in favour of a decree-holder, that decree-holder must be paid from the sale proceeds before those proceeds are distributed rateably among other creditors.
material_facts: The properties were sold in execution of a decree ordering sale to discharge the charge in favour of the appellant.
The proceeds of the sale were held by the court.
The respondents were simple money creditors seeking rateable distribution of the proceeds.
issues.conclusion: The sale expenses and the amount due to the appellant had to be paid first; only the balance could be distributed among the respondents.
issues.legal_principle: Section 73(1), proviso (c), of the Code of Civil Procedure applies where immovable property is sold in execution of a decree ordering sale for the discharge of an encumbrance. After sale expenses, the proceeds must first discharge the amount due to the decree-holder for whose benefit the encumbrance is enforced; only the remaining balance is available for rateable distribution.

predicates.rateable_distribution_proceeding: Creditors applied to share assets realized through execution of a decree.
predicates.property_sold_under_encumbrance_discharg: Property was sold under a decree ordering its sale to discharge an encumbrance.
predicates.claimant_holds_encumbrance_for_sale: A decree-holder had the benefit of the encumbrance that the sale was ordered to discharge.

issues.definition: When property is sold under a decree to discharge an encumbrance, the decree-holder whose encumbrance is being discharged is paid before other creditors share any remaining proceeds.
